questions.prompt: What is the core move in Greene's nonengagement strategy?
choices: Fight immediately before the stronger side settles
Yield exposed ground and buy time instead of fighting on stronger terms
Hide your real intention until after losing the first battle

explanation.gentle: The chapter is about refusing battle on the stronger side's preferred ground.
explanation.direct: Start with the mechanism: trade space for time rather than absorb superior force head-on.
explanation.competitive: Nonengagement means leaving the kill zone before it kills the campaign.

questions.prompt: What is really being bought when space is traded in this chapter?
choices: Public admiration
More allies immediately
Time for rebuilding, repositioning, or waiting for overextension

explanation.gentle: The ground matters because of the time it can create.
explanation.direct: Notice the real asset: time that can be spent productively later.
explanation.competitive: The retreat is paying for clock, not for dignity.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter's main reversal about strategic depth?
choices: Withdrawal always creates new options
Strategic depth matters only in military settings
If there is no fallback depth, retreat may become liquidation

explanation.gentle: The chapter only works where something can be given up safely.
explanation.direct: The reversal is simple: no depth means no safe trade of space for time.
explanation.competitive: No second field means the retreat may end the war instead of saving it.

questions.prompt: Joelle is facing a giant in a prestige segment her startup cannot afford to defend. What fits the chapter best?
choices: Stay and match the spending race so outsiders see resolve
Exit early, preserve capital, and strengthen a weaker flank for later competition
Wait until the company is almost out of cash before deciding

explanation.gentle: Joelle needs to preserve the company, not the optics of the segment.
explanation.direct: Joelle uses nonengagement correctly when retreat preserves force for better terrain later.
explanation.competitive: Leave the giant's arena before it turns your balance sheet into rubble.

questions.prompt: Why does Malik decline the public forum with the better resourced rival team?
choices: Because he has no opinion on the issue
Because the forum serves the rival's timing and resources more than the work
Because he wants to avoid all future hearings

explanation.gentle: Malik is refusing a venue that favors the stronger side right now.
explanation.direct: The chapter backs Malik because he is trading weak optics for a better later field.
explanation.competitive: He denies them the stage built for his loss.

questions.prompt: Briony can only survive by leaving one market segment a giant now dominates. What is the strategic logic?
choices: Giving up bad ground can preserve the larger campaign
Every retreat guarantees later victory
Prestige markets should never be abandoned

explanation.gentle: Briony is choosing campaign survival over symbolic presence.
explanation.direct: The move works because the surrendered segment is less valuable than the force it would consume.
explanation.competitive: Lose the lane if it saves the war chest.

questions.prompt: Cyrus is stuck on one contract point the stronger side can defend forever. What does the chapter suggest?
choices: Keep escalating on that point because retreat always looks weak
Trade the exposed point if doing so preserves the larger negotiation
Walk away from all future deals entirely

explanation.gentle: One surrendered point can keep a larger objective alive.
explanation.direct: Cyrus uses nonengagement when he gives up the unwinnable position to save the rest.
explanation.competitive: Drop the trapped inch if it keeps the contract breathing.

questions.prompt: Why does retreat fail for Elian in the single-opportunity fellowship case?
choices: Because he lacked strategic depth and the position was the whole doorway
Because retreat is always unethical
Because stronger rivals always respect delay

explanation.gentle: Elian had no real fallback behind the withdrawal.
explanation.direct: The strategy fails because there was no depth to trade safely.
explanation.competitive: He stepped back off the only ledge he had.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter's main ethical danger in using retreat badly?
choices: Retreat can become an excuse for avoiding necessary struggle
Retreat always destroys reputation permanently
Retreat removes all responsibility for later action

explanation.gentle: The chapter goes weak when withdrawal protects comfort more than the campaign.
explanation.direct: Ethically, the warning is against dressing fear or drift up as strategy.
explanation.competitive: A fake retreat is just avoidance wearing military language.

questions.prompt: What has to happen after Chapter 11 buys time for the operator?
choices: The operator should stay defensive forever
The surrendered ground should be forgotten completely
The saved interval has to be used in service of a larger strategic design

explanation.gentle: Chapter 12 asks what longer war the bought time is actually serving.
explanation.direct: The bridge forward is grand strategy: saved time has to be spent on a larger design.
explanation.competitive: The clock matters only if it feeds the next offensive plan.
